summary: A 1970 set of notes by E. Meyer from a network meeting.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 82 summarizes three network meetings held in Houston in November 1970. The notes cover protocol changes, terminal communication, file transfer and the Network Information Center, and the author cautions that his summary may be biased.

subtitle: A record of discussions at three Network Working Group meetings in Houston.

tldr.problem: The meeting notes cover protocol, operational and coordination questions raised as network sites began using the ARPANET.
tldr.mechanism: Edwin Meyer summarizes discussions from three meetings during the 1970 Fall Joint Computer Conference, including terminal interaction, protocol work, file transfer and documentation services.
tldr.outcome: The notes record proposals, disagreements and planned work; the author warns that his summary may be biased or may misunderstand parts of the discussions.

sections.title: Three Meetings and Their Limits
sections.content:
Edwin Meyer says he transcribed the summary from notes taken at three Network Working Group meetings in Houston during the 1970 Fall Joint Computer Conference. He warns that the account is unavoidably biased by his interests and may misunderstand or distort some statements.

The notes record topics and discussion rather than a set of formal decisions.
sections.plainLanguage: The document summarizes three meetings from the note-taker's perspective. He warns readers that some parts may be incomplete or mistaken.

sections.title: Protocol and Host Communication
sections.content:
The Monday discussion lists NCP testing, reworking error control and flow control, handling overload, and simplifying or relayering the protocol as areas of concern. Participants disagree about when to change the basic protocol and emphasize the need for operational use.

Later discussion examines console communication, including local echo, full- or half-duplex operation, character-by-character input and line-oriented input. Participants also discuss message boundaries, line formats and how terminal input should be represented, without settling every issue.
sections.plainLanguage: The attendees discuss how to test and improve the network protocol and how different terminals should communicate. The notes show disagreement and open questions rather than a final design.

sections.title: The Network Information Center
sections.content:
Doug Engelbart describes the Network Information Center as a service for collecting documents, cataloging and indexing them, and providing access. The discussion includes hard-copy material, online catalogs, and local collections containing a useful subset of a master collection.

The notes also describe a Network Dialogue System of human agents: a technical communications agent and a technical liaison at each site. The participants discuss how sites could exchange reference information and provide documentation about their systems.
sections.plainLanguage: The NIC discussion focuses on helping sites find documents and information about other hosts. It also describes people at each site who would help answer questions and exchange material.

sections.title: File Transfer and Further Work
sections.content:
The later meetings discuss how to send files, represent records, mark the end of a file and separate control information from data. Several approaches are raised, including record counts, an end-of-file packet, closing a connection and separate data and control connections.

The final meeting notes that issues remain unsettled and calls for proposals to be written before further discussion. The document records the debate, not a single adopted file-transfer method.
sections.plainLanguage: The participants consider several ways to send files and mark where they end. The notes leave these questions open and call for written proposals.
